Chapter 1: AI and the Future of Engineering
Artificial Intelligence is transforming every domain of engineering — but not in the way most news headlines 
suggest. The narrative that "AI will replace all engineers" is both correct and deeply misleading at the same  
time. Understanding exactly what is happening, and what is not happening, is the most important thing you  
can do for your career right now.
1.1 What AI Is Actually Replacing
AI is replacing specific tasks, not entire professions. More precisely, it is replacing tasks that are repetitive,  
pattern-based, and do not require physical interaction with the real world. The jobs that are disappearing first 
are:
● Data entry and basic report generation — AI can read, extract, and summarise structured data faster 
than any human
● Generic CRUD application development — AI can write a basic REST API or a React component in 
seconds
● Basic QA testing — AI can generate test cases and run regression tests automatically
● Junior content writing — AI can produce first drafts of documentation, emails, and reports
● Simple data analysis — AI can compute statistics, plot graphs, and find correlations without a data 
analyst
Notice what is NOT on that list: physical hardware engineering, sensor integration, real-time embedded  
systems, anything requiring a physical presence, and domain-specific expertise that took years to build. This is 
exactly where AIoT engineering lives.
1.2 Why AIoT Engineers Are Safe — And In Demand
AIoT (Artificial Intelligence of Things) sits at the intersection of three domains that AI cannot fully automate:  
physical hardware, embedded software, and machine learning. Here is why each layer protects you:
Layer 1 — Physical Hardware
Sensors, microcontrollers, Raspberry Pi boards, motors, and industrial machines exist in the physical world. An 
AI cannot solder a circuit, debug a faulty sensor reading caused by electromagnetic interference, or physically 
install an edge device in a factory. Your EEE diploma gives you exactly this physical engineering foundation that 
pure software engineers lack entirely.
Layer 2 — Embedded Software
Writing real-time code that runs on a device with 512MB of RAM, no swap space, and a hard latency  
requirement of 50ms is not something a generic AI tool handles well. It requires knowledge of Linux internals, 
memory management, and hardware-specific drivers. This expertise takes years to develop.
Layer 3 — Domain ML
Training a general image classification model is easy. Training a model that detects a specific type of bearing  
wear in a factory machine, on noisy sensor data, with limited labelled examples, while running on a Raspberry 
Pi at 15 FPS — that requires deep domain knowledge. AI tools help you write the code, but you must know  
what to ask them to write.

Note: 📌 The engineer who gets replaced is the one who writes boilerplate code all day without 
understanding the domain. The engineer who thrives is the one who uses AI to eliminate boilerplate and 
focus entirely on the hard domain problems only they can solve.
1.3 The AI Augmentation Model — Your Mental Framework
Instead of thinking "AI vs Engineer", adopt the framework of AI Augmentation. Every task you do falls into one 
of three categories:
Task Type Example Your Role AI Role
Automate fully Writing boilerplate code Define what you want Write the code
AI-assisted Debugging a sensor 
driver
Know what is wrong Suggest fixes
Human only Hardware integration + 
testing
Do everything Cannot help
Your goal over the next 4 years is to push as many tasks as possible into the first two categories, so you spend 
almost all your time on the third category — the work only you can do.
1.4 The Three AI Skills Every Engineer Needs Now
Regardless of domain, every engineer in 2026 needs exactly three AI-related skills. Without them, you will fall 
behind even within your own specialisation.
Skill 1: Prompt Engineering
The ability to communicate precisely with an AI model to get exactly the output you need. This is the new  
"knowing how to use Google" — it seems trivial but there is enormous variation in how effectively different  
people use AI tools. A well-crafted prompt can get you a complete, working, production-quality solution. A  
poorly crafted prompt wastes 30 minutes.
Skill 2: AI-Assisted Development (Vibe Coding)
Using AI code editors like Cursor to write code by describing what you want in natural language, reviewing the 
output critically, and iterating. The critical review part is non-negotiable — if you cannot review AI-generated 
code, you will ship broken systems. This is why your DSA and Python fundamentals still matter enormously.
Skill 3: AI Agent Building
Creating small autonomous systems that use an LLM as their reasoning engine to complete multi-step tasks.  
For an AIoT engineer, this means agents that monitor sensor data, detect anomalies, and trigger responses  
automatically — without human intervention for every decision.

1.5 The Japan AIoT Market — Why Your Timing Is Perfect
Japan is undergoing the largest industrial automation transformation in its history. The country has a severe  
labour shortage due to an ageing population, and the government has set national targets for factory  
automation, smart infrastructure, and agricultural robotics. This is creating extraordinary demand for  
engineers who combine:
● Embedded systems and hardware knowledge (your EEE diploma)
● AI/ML for edge deployment (your PyTorch + TFLite path)
● IoT connectivity and protocols (MQTT, OPC-UA — your Month 3-4 learning)
● Japanese language ability (your JLPT path to N2)
The overlap of all four qualifications in a single engineer is genuinely rare. Japanese companies like Panasonic, 
Omron, Hitachi, Fanuc, Keyence, and dozens of mid-size manufacturers are actively competing for this profile. 
Your 2029 target is not ambitious — it is well-timed.
 Tip: 💡 When you reach Japan, emphasise your EEE background in every interview. Japanese 
manufacturing engineers deeply respect hardware knowledge. An Indian engineer who can both write 
Edge AI code AND understand the machine it is controlling is someone they have not seen before.

Chapter 2: Vibe Coding and Cursor IDE — Complete Guide
Vibe coding is the practice of building software by describing what you want in natural language and letting an 
AI code editor generate the implementation. The term was coined in early 2025 and describes a workflow that 
has become the dominant way professional engineers write code in 2026.
2.1 What Is Cursor IDE
Cursor is an AI-first code editor built on top of VS Code. It uses large language models (Claude, GPT-4, and  
others) to understand your codebase and generate code in context. Unlike GitHub Copilot which only  
autocompletes, Cursor can:
● Generate entire files from a description
● Refactor existing code while preserving logic
● Debug errors by reading your error message and suggesting fixes
● Answer questions about any part of your codebase
● Apply multi-file edits in one command
● Connect to MCP servers to call external tools
 Note: 📌 Cursor is free for 2000 completions per month. The Pro plan ($20/month) gives unlimited 
completions. Start with the free plan — it is more than enough for learning.
2.2 Installation and Setup
Step 1: Download and Install
Download Cursor from cursor.com. It installs exactly like VS Code. On first launch, it asks you to import your  
existing VS Code settings — do this. All your themes, extensions, and keybindings carry over.
Step 2: Choose Your AI Model
Cursor supports multiple models. For your use case, use Claude Sonnet 4.6 (best for code generation and  
reasoning) or GPT-4o (faster, slightly less accurate). Switch between them with Ctrl+/ in the chat panel.
Step 3: Index Your Project
When you open a folder, Cursor indexes the entire codebase. This allows the AI to understand imports,  
function signatures, and data structures across files. For a Raspberry Pi project, open the entire project folder 
— not individual files.
Step 4: Configure Cursor Rules
Cursor Rules are instructions that apply to every AI interaction in a project. Create a file called .cursorrules in 
your project root. For your AIoT projects, use this template:
You are an expert AIoT engineer specialising in Edge AI and Raspberry Pi 
development.
Always write Python code compatible with Python 3.10+ and Raspberry Pi OS.
Use TensorFlow Lite for all model inference — never full TensorFlow.
Use paho-mqtt for all MQTT communication.

Add type hints to every function. Add docstrings to every class and function.
When writing sensor code, always include error handling for I2C and SPI failures.
Prefer async patterns for I/O-heavy operations.
2.3 The Five Core Cursor Features
Feature 1: Ctrl+K — Inline Edit
Select any block of code and press Ctrl+K to open an inline prompt. Describe what you want to change. Cursor 
applies the edit directly. This is the fastest way to refactor existing code.
Feature 2: Ctrl+L — Chat Panel
Opens a full chat panel where you can ask questions about your code, request new features, or debug  
problems. The chat has full context of your entire indexed codebase.
Feature 3: Ctrl+I — Composer (Agent Mode)
The most powerful feature. Describe a complete feature or project and Cursor will create and edit multiple files 
automatically. It shows you each change before applying it. Use this for building entire modules.
Feature 4: @ Mentions
In any chat message, type @ to reference specific files, folders, or documentation. Example: "Refactor  
@sensor_reader.py to use async/await based on the pattern in @utils.py". This gives the AI precise context.
Feature 5: Codebase-wide Search
Ask "How does the MQTT connection get established in this project?" and Cursor searches the entire codebase 
to find the answer. Essential for understanding unfamiliar code.
2.4 Effective Prompt Patterns for AIoT Code
The quality of your prompt directly determines the quality of the output. Here are the prompt patterns that  
work best for AIoT engineering:
Pattern 1: Role + Task + Constraints
Act as an embedded Python developer. Write a sensor reader class for DHT22
on Raspberry Pi GPIO pin 4. Requirements: (1) read every 5 seconds (2) handle
sensor failures gracefully (3) return a dataclass with temperature, humidity,
timestamp (4) log errors to a file (5) compatible with Python 3.10+
Pattern 2: Provide Example Input/Output
I need a function that converts raw ADC readings to engineering units.
Input example: {"raw": 2048, "sensor": "pressure", "range_min": 0, "range_max": 10}
Output example: {"value": 5.0, "unit": "bar", "timestamp": "2026-09-07T17:30:00"}
Write the function with full type hints and unit tests.

Pattern 3: Iterative Refinement
Never try to get the perfect result in one prompt. Start broad, then refine:
● Prompt 1: "Write a basic MQTT publisher for sensor data"
● Prompt 2: "Add reconnection logic with exponential backoff"
● Prompt 3: "Add a message queue so data is not lost during disconnection"
● Prompt 4: "Add unit tests for the queue logic"
 Tip: 💡 Treat Cursor like a junior developer who is very fast but needs clear instructions. If the output is 
wrong, do not rewrite it manually — explain what is wrong and ask Cursor to fix it. This trains you to give 
better prompts.
2.5 Vibe Coding Workflow for AIoT Projects
Here is the exact workflow to use for every AIoT project you build:
Step 1: Write a PRD (Product Requirements Document)
Before writing any code, create a file called PRD.md in your project folder and describe exactly what you are  
building. Include: what problem it solves, what hardware it uses, what software components it needs, and  
what the expected output is. Cursor will use this as context for every code generation request.
Step 2: Generate the Project Structure
Open Composer (Ctrl+I) and type:
"Read PRD.md and create the complete project structure with
empty files, a requirements.txt, and a README.md"
Step 3: Implement Module by Module
Generate each module separately. Do not try to generate the entire project at once. Start with the sensor  
reading module, then the data processing module, then the MQTT publisher, then the dashboard.
Step 4: Test Each Module
Ask Cursor: "Write unit tests for sensor_reader.py using pytest.
Mock the GPIO pins so tests run on a laptop without a Raspberry Pi."
Step 5: Integration and Debugging
When something breaks, paste the full error message into Cursor chat. Never try to debug without sharing the 
full traceback. Cursor needs the complete error context to suggest accurate fixes.

Chapter 3: Claude API and Prompt Engineering
The Claude API gives you programmatic access to Anthropic's Claude models from any Python script. For an  
AIoT engineer, this is the most powerful tool available — it lets you add AI reasoning to any part of your system: 
sensor data analysis, anomaly explanation, automated reporting, and natural language interfaces to your  
hardware.
3.1 Getting Started with the Claude API
Installation:
pip install anthropic python-dotenv
API Key Setup:

ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-your-key-here
# In Python

First API Call:

    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,

weeks of learning and experimentation.
3.2 System Prompts — The Most Powerful Feature
A system prompt is a set of instructions you give Claude before the conversation begins. It defines Claude's  
role, constraints, and output format. For AIoT applications, system prompts are how you turn a general AI into 
a domain-specific expert.
AIoT Sensor Analyst System Prompt:
system = """You are an expert AIoT systems engineer specialising in
industrial sensor data analysis. You have deep knowledge of:

- Sensor physics (temperature, pressure, vibration, current)
- Normal operating ranges for industrial equipment
- Failure modes and their sensor signatures
- Statistical anomaly detection methods
When analysing sensor data:
1. Always state the normal range for the sensor type
2. Identify any anomalies with confidence level (High/Medium/Low)
3. Suggest the most likely physical cause
4. Recommend immediate action if safety-critical
5. Format output as JSON for programmatic processing
Be concise and technical. Use engineering units correctly."""
3.3 Complete AIoT Sensor Analysis Application
This is the complete code for an AI-powered sensor analyst — the project from your first Sunday session. Study 
every line.
import anthropic
import json
import csv
import os
from datetime import datetime
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are an AIoT sensor analysis expert.
Analyse sensor readings and detect anomalies.
Always respond with valid JSON only, no other text.
Format: {"status": "normal|warning|critical",
"anomalies": [], "analysis": "", "action": ""}"""
def read_sensor_log(filepath: str, last_n: int = 10) -> list[dict]:
    """Read last N rows from sensor CSV log."""
    with open(filepath, newline="") as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    return rows[-last_n:]
def analyse_sensors(readings: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Send readings to Claude for AI analysis."""

user_message = f"""Analyse these sensor readings:
    {json.dumps(readings, indent=2)}
    Identify anomalies. Return JSON only."""
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1000,
        system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]
    )
    return json.loads(response.content[0].text)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    readings = read_sensor_log("sensor_log.csv", last_n=10)
    result = analyse_sensors(readings)
    print(f"Status: {result['status'].upper()}")
    print(f"Analysis: {result['analysis']}")
    if result["action"]:
        print(f"ACTION REQUIRED: {result['action']}")
3.4 Prompt Engineering — Complete Reference
Prompt engineering is the skill of crafting inputs to AI models that reliably produce the output you need. It is a 
skill with real depth — the difference between a novice and expert prompt engineer is 10x output quality.
Principle 1: Be Specific About Format
Vague: "Analyse the sensor data." — you will get a paragraph of text.
Specific:  "Analyse  the  sensor  data.  Respond  ONLY  with  a  JSON  object  containing:  status  
(normal/warning/critical), anomalies (array of strings), confidence (0-1 float)."
Principle 2: Provide Context Before the Task
# Bad prompt
"Is this temperature reading normal?"
# Good prompt
"Context: Industrial motor bearing sensor. Normal range: 60-80°C.
Critical threshold: >100°C. Is this reading normal? Temperature: 94°C.
Respond with: {normal: bool, risk_level: low/medium/high, reason: str}"
Principle 3: Chain of Thought for Complex Reasoning
prompt = """Analyse this sensor trend. Think step by step:
Step 1: What is the baseline (first 5 readings)?
Step 2: What is the current value?

Step 3: What is the rate of change?
Step 4: Based on the rate of change, when will it reach critical threshold?
Data: {data}
After your step-by-step analysis, give a final JSON summary."""
Principle 4: Few-Shot Examples
prompt = """Classify sensor alerts. Examples:
Input: temp=45°C, normal_max=40°C, rate=+0.5°C/min
Output: {"severity": "warning", "time_to_critical": "10min"}
Input: temp=38°C, normal_max=40°C, rate=-0.1°C/min
Output: {"severity": "normal", "time_to_critical": null}
Now classify this:
Input: temp={temp}°C, normal_max={max}°C, rate={rate}°C/min"""
3.5 Multi-Turn Conversations — Memory for AIoT Agents
By default, each Claude API call has no memory of previous calls. For a persistent AIoT monitoring agent, you 
need to maintain conversation history manually.
class AIoTAgent:
    def __init__(self, system_prompt: str):
        self.client = anthropic.Anthropic()
        self.system = system_prompt
        self.history = []  # maintains conversation memory
    def analyse(self, sensor_data: dict) -> str:
        user_msg = f"New reading: {json.dumps(sensor_data)}"
        self.history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_msg})
        response = self.client.messages.create(
            model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
            max_tokens=500,
            system=self.system,
            messages=self.history
        )
        reply = response.content[0].text
        self.history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})
        # Trim history to last 20 messages to control token costs
        if len(self.history) > 20:
            self.history = self.history[-20:]

return reply

Chapter 5: LangChain and AI Agents
LangChain is a Python framework for building applications powered by large language models. It provides  
abstractions for memory, tool use, chains of reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). For AIoT, 
LangChain allows you to build agents that reason over your sensor data, call your APIs, and take autonomous 
actions.
5.1 Core LangChain Concepts
LLMs and Chat Models
LangChain wraps different LLM providers (Claude, GPT, Gemini) behind a unified interface. This means you can 
switch from Claude to GPT with one line change — a significant advantage when cost or capability  
requirements change.
Chains
A chain is a sequence of operations. Input → LLM → Output. Or Input → Prompt Template → LLM → Output  
Parser → Structured Data. Chains are the building blocks of every LangChain application.
Memory
LangChain provides built-in memory modules that maintain conversation history automatically. For an AIoT  
monitoring agent, this means the agent remembers that "the temperature was rising last hour" without you  
manually tracking state.
Tools and Agents
An agent is an LLM that can decide which tools to call based on the user's request. You give it a set of tools  
(functions it can call), and it decides the sequence of tool calls needed to complete a task. For AIoT, tools  
include: read_sensor_data(), query_database(), send_alert(), control_actuator().
5.2 Installation
pip install langchain langchain-anthropic langchain-community
pip install chromadb  # for vector database
pip install pymongo   # for MongoDB tool
5.3 Your First LangChain AIoT Agent
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain.agents import create_tool_calling_agent, AgentExecutor
from langchain.tools import tool
from langchain.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from pymongo import MongoClient
import json
# Connect to your MongoDB Atlas
mongo = MongoClient("your-atlas-connection-string")

db = mongo["aiot_database"]
# Define tools the agent can use
@tool
def get_latest_readings(sensor_location: str) -> str:
    """Get the latest 5 sensor readings for a location."""
    readings = list(db.sensors.find(
        {"location": sensor_location},
        sort=[("timestamp", -1)], limit=5
    ))
    return json.dumps(readings, default=str)
@tool
def get_anomaly_count(hours: int = 24) -> str:
    """Get count of anomalies in the last N hours."""
    from datetime import datetime, timedelta
    since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=hours)
    count = db.alerts.count_documents({"timestamp": {"$gte": since}})
    return f"{count} anomalies detected in last {hours} hours"
# Create the agent
llm = ChatAnthropic(model="claude-sonnet-4-6")
tools = [get_latest_readings, get_anomaly_count]
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are an AIoT monitoring expert. Use tools to answer."),
    ("human", "{input}"),
    ("placeholder", "{agent_scratchpad}"),
])
agent = create_tool_calling_agent(llm, tools, prompt)
executor = AgentExecutor(agent=agent, tools=tools, verbose=True)
# Natural language query
result = executor.invoke({"input": "How many anomalies in Zone 3 today?"})
print(result["output"])
5.4 RAG — Make AI Read Your Sensor Logs
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) allows an AI model to answer questions based on your own  
documents and data — not just its training data. For AIoT, this means you can ask "What caused the last 3  
shutdowns of Machine 7?" and get an answer derived from your actual maintenance logs and sensor history.

How RAG works:
● Step 1: Your documents (sensor logs, maintenance records) are split into chunks
● Step 2: Each chunk is converted to a vector embedding (numerical representation)
● Step 3: Embeddings are stored in a vector database (ChromaDB, Pinecone)
● Step 4: User asks a question → question is also embedded
● Step 5: Most similar document chunks are retrieved
● Step 6: Retrieved chunks + question are sent to Claude for a grounded answer
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic
from langchain_community.vectorstores import Chroma
from langchain_anthropic import AnthropicEmbeddings
from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

6.2 The Edge AI Workflow: Train → Convert → Deploy
Phase 1: Train in PyTorch or Keras
You train your model on a powerful computer (laptop, cloud GPU, Google Colab) using full PyTorch or  
TensorFlow. This is your familiar Python ML workflow. Model accuracy and architecture are optimised here.
Phase 2: Convert to TFLite
TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) is a compressed, optimised format for running models on embedded devices. The  
conversion process applies quantisation (reducing weight precision from 32-bit float to 8-bit integer) which  
reduces model size by 4x and inference speed by 2-3x with minimal accuracy loss.
Phase 3: Deploy on Pi
The TFLite model (.tflite file) is copied to the Raspberry Pi. The TFLite runtime interprets the model and runs  
inference. No internet connection required. No GPU required for most models.

import tflite_runtime.interpreter as tflite
import numpy as np

import time
def load_model(model_path: str):
    interpreter = tflite.Interpreter(model_path=model_path)
    interpreter.allocate_tensors()
    return interpreter
def run_inference(interpreter, input_data: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    input_details = interpreter.get_input_details()
    output_details = interpreter.get_output_details()
    interpreter.set_tensor(input_details[0]["index"], input_data)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    interpreter.invoke()
    latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
    output = interpreter.get_tensor(output_details[0]["index"])
    return output, latency_ms
# Load model once at startup
interpreter = load_model("model.tflite")
# Run inference on new sensor reading
sensor_data = np.array([[25.3, 62.1, 1.2, ...]], dtype=np.float32)
prediction, latency = run_inference(interpreter, sensor_data)
class_idx = np.argmax(prediction)
classes = ["normal", "warning", "fault", "critical"]

    dummy = np.random.rand(1, 10).astype(np.float32)

interpreter.set_tensor(input_details[0]["index"], dummy)

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import json, time, logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class MQTTConfig:
    host: str = "localhost"
    port: int = 1883
    keepalive: int = 60
    client_id: str = "aiot_edge_001"
    username: str = None
    password: str = None
class RobustMQTTClient:
    """Production MQTT client with auto-reconnect."""
    def __init__(self, config: MQTTConfig):

self.config = config
        self.client = mqtt.Client(config.client_id)
        self.client.on_connect = self._on_connect
        self.client.on_disconnect = self._on_disconnect
        self.client.on_message = self._on_message
        if config.username:
            self.client.username_pw_set(config.username, config.password)
        # Will message — sent if connection drops unexpectedly
        self.client.will_set(f"status/{config.client_id}",
            json.dumps({"status": "offline", "reason": "unexpected"}),
            qos=1, retain=True)
    def _on_connect(self, client, userdata, flags, rc):
        if rc == 0:
            logging.info("MQTT connected")
            # Publish online status
            client.publish(f"status/{self.config.client_id}",
                json.dumps({"status": "online"}), qos=1, retain=True)
            # Re-subscribe after reconnection
            client.subscribe("sensors/#", qos=1)
        else:
            logging.error(f"MQTT connect failed: rc={rc}")
    def _on_disconnect(self, client, userdata, rc):
        if rc != 0:
            logging.warning("Unexpected disconnect, reconnecting...")
            # paho auto-reconnects if loop_start() is used
    def _on_message(self, client, userdata, msg):
        try:
            payload = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
            self.process_message(msg.topic, payload)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            logging.error(f"Invalid JSON on {msg.topic}: {e}")
    def process_message(self, topic: str, payload: dict):
        """Override this method in subclasses."""
        print(f"[{topic}] {payload}")
    def start(self):
        self.client.connect(self.config.host, self.config.port, 
self.config.keepalive)
        self.client.loop_start()  # non-blocking background thread

Nemawashi (根回し) — Consensus Building

In Japanese companies, decisions are made by building consensus before any formal meeting. Before  
proposing a new idea, speak to each stakeholder individually and get their informal agreement. Walking into a 
meeting with a surprise proposal is considered disrespectful.
Kaizen (改善) — Continuous Improvement
Every Japanese manufacturing company runs on kaizen principles. You are expected to proactively identify  
small improvements in your workflow and suggest them. This is not optional — it is part of the job. Write down 
1 kaizen suggestion per week as a habit.
Horenso (報連相) — Report, Contact, Consult
Always report your progress to your supervisor (  報 告 - houkoku). Contact immediately when something  
unexpected happens (  連絡 - renraku). Consult your supervisor before making any independent decision (相談 
- soudan). Following this framework makes you a trusted team member quickly.
Japanese Email Etiquette
Business emails in Japanese follow a strict format: greeting formula → identity → context → main content → 
closing formula. Study this format before starting work. Your N2 Japanese will handle conversation — email  
formality is a separate skill.

    if reading.sensor_type in THRESHOLDS:

D.1 Technical Interview Question Bank — AIoT Roles
Category 1: Python and Machine Learning
● Explain the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning with an IoT example.
○ Answer: Supervised — classify sensor readings as normal/fault using labelled historical data. 
Unsupervised — cluster sensor patterns to find unknown failure modes.
● What is a neural network? Explain forward and backward pass.
● What is overfitting and how do you prevent it?
○ Answer: Model performs well on training data but poorly on new data. Prevention: dropout, 
regularisation (L2), data augmentation, early stopping.
● Explain the difference between batch normalisation and layer normalisation.
● What is transfer learning? Give an AIoT example.
○ Answer: Use a pre-trained MobileNet (trained on ImageNet) and fine-tune on your specific 
factory defect images. Much less data required.
● What is the purpose of the softmax function?
● Explain gradient descent. What is the learning rate?
Category 2: Edge AI and Hardware
● What is model quantisation? What are the tradeoffs?
○ Answer: Reducing weight precision from FP32 to INT8. Tradeoffs: 4x smaller model, 2-3x 
faster inference, slight accuracy reduction (typically <2%).
● What is the difference between TFLite and ONNX Runtime?
○ Answer: TFLite is TensorFlow-specific, highly optimised for ARM processors. ONNX Runtime 
is framework-agnostic (PyTorch, TF, sklearn), runs on more hardware types.
● How would you optimise inference speed on a Raspberry Pi?
○ Answer: INT8 quantisation, smaller model (MobileNet vs ResNet), reduce input resolution, 
use NEON SIMD instructions, profile with TFLite Benchmark Tool.
● What is the difference between I2C and SPI? When do you use each?
○ Answer: I2C uses 2 wires (SDA, SCL), slower but multiple devices on same bus. SPI uses 4 
wires (MISO, MOSI, SCK, CS), faster, used for displays and high-speed ADCs.
● What happens if a Raspberry Pi loses internet during Edge AI inference?
○ Answer: Inference continues normally — TFLite runs locally. MQTT publishing fails. 
Implement a local queue that buffers data and sends when connection restores.
Category 3: IoT and Protocols
● Explain MQTT QoS levels. When do you use each?
○ QoS 0: Fire and forget — high-frequency sensor data where loss is acceptable. QoS 1: Alert 
messages — at least once delivery. QoS 2: Actuator commands — exactly once, critical.
● What is a message broker? How does Mosquitto work?
● Explain the publish-subscribe pattern vs request-response. When is each better?
○ Pub/Sub: IoT sensors (many publishers, many subscribers, decoupled). Request/Response: 
REST API (client needs immediate response to a specific query).
● What is a retained message in MQTT?

○ Answer: The broker stores the last message on a topic. New subscribers immediately receive 
this value — useful for device status (online/offline) that rarely changes.
Category 4: System Design for AIoT
● Design an IoT system that monitors 1000 sensors in a factory.
○ Answer template: Sensors → MQTT with QoS 1 → Edge Pi per zone (batch processing, local 
TFLite) → aggregated MQTT to central broker → MongoDB Atlas → Dashboard + Alerting
● How would you ensure your AIoT system works during internet outages?
○ Answer: Edge processing on Pi (no cloud needed for inference), local SQLite buffering during 
outage, sync to Atlas on reconnect using change streams.
● How would you handle 10ms inference latency requirements?
○ Answer: MobileNetV3-Small with INT8 quantisation achieves 8-12ms on Pi 4. If not enough: 
NVIDIA Jetson Nano for GPU acceleration, or resize input to 128x128.

def train_model(model, train_loader, val_loader, epochs=10, lr=1e-3):
    """Production training loop with validation, early stopping, logging."""
    device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    model = model.to(device)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
    optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, patience=3)
    best_val_loss = float("inf")
    patience_counter = 0
    history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": [], "val_acc": []}
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        # ── TRAINING PHASE ──
        model.train()
        train_loss = 0.0
        for batch_X, batch_y in train_loader:
            batch_X, batch_y = batch_X.to(device), batch_y.to(device)
            optimizer.zero_grad()             # clear previous gradients
            outputs = model(batch_X)          # forward pass
            loss = criterion(outputs, batch_y) # compute loss
            loss.backward()                   # backpropagation
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) # prevent 
gradient explosion
            optimizer.step()                  # update weights
            train_loss += loss.item()
        # ── VALIDATION PHASE ──
        model.eval()
        val_loss, correct, total = 0.0, 0, 0
        with torch.no_grad():                 # no gradient tracking needed
            for batch_X, batch_y in val_loader:
                batch_X, batch_y = batch_X.to(device), batch_y.to(device)
                outputs = model(batch_X)
                val_loss += criterion(outputs, batch_y).item()
                _, predicted = outputs.max(1)
                total += batch_y.size(0)
                correct += predicted.eq(batch_y).sum().item()
        avg_train = train_loss / len(train_loader)
        avg_val = val_loss / len(val_loader)
        val_acc = 100.0 * correct / total
        scheduler.step(avg_val)

history["train_loss"].append(avg_train)
        history["val_loss"].append(avg_val)
        history["val_acc"].append(val_acc)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs} | Train: {avg_train:.4f} | Val: 
{avg_val:.4f} | Acc: {val_acc:.2f}%")
        # ── EARLY STOPPING ──
        if avg_val < best_val_loss:
            best_val_loss = avg_val
            torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best_model.pth")
            patience_counter = 0
        else:
            patience_counter += 1
            if patience_counter >= 5:
                print(f"Early stopping at epoch {epoch+1}")
                break
    return history

2.2 What "Agentic AI" Really Means For Your Work (Simple Explanation)
You will hear the word "agentic" everywhere in 2026. Let us understand it simply.
OLD WAY (non-agentic):
● You write code that does exactly what you tell it
● If sensor reads 45°C, send email — you program every single rule
● When a new situation happens that you did not program, the system fails
NEW WAY (agentic AI):
● You give the AI a goal: "Keep the factory running safely"
● The AI decides HOW to achieve that goal using available tools
● When a new situation happens, the AI reasons about what to do
● The AI can learn from past events to handle new ones better
  ANALOGY — Security Guard: 🔄 Non-agentic AI is like giving a security guard a list of rules: "If door 
opens at night, call police. If fire alarm sounds, call fire station." They only follow the list. Agentic AI is like 
hiring an experienced security guard who uses judgment. When something new happens (a suspicious 
smell), they figure out the best response without needing a pre-written rule for it.

In your AIoT context, agentic AI means:
● Instead of hard-coded threshold rules (if temp > 40, alert), you have an AI that understands the 
CONTEXT
● The AI knows: "This machine normally runs hot after noon because of sun exposure — 42°C is fine 
here"
● The AI knows: "But if this is a Tuesday and cooling was just serviced, 42°C is suspicious"
● This contextual reasoning is what makes agentic AI so powerful and so hard to replicate with simple 
rules
  NOTE: 📌 This is why LangChain memory matters so much. Memory gives the agent CONTEXT. Without 
memory, every sensor reading is isolated. With memory, the agent understands history and patterns — 
like an experienced human engineer would.

# monitor.py — Smart Temperature Monitor
import time, smtplib, logging
import adafruit_dht
import board
from email.mime.text import MIMEText
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os
load_dotenv()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(message)s")
# ── SETTINGS ── (change these to your values)
ALERT_TEMP    = 35.0          # alert if temperature exceeds this
CHECK_INTERVAL = 10           # seconds between readings
EMAIL_FROM    = os.getenv("EMAIL_FROM")
EMAIL_TO      = os.getenv("EMAIL_TO")
EMAIL_PASS    = os.getenv("EMAIL_PASS")
# ── SENSOR SETUP ──
dht = adafruit_dht.DHT22(board.D4)   # GPIO pin 4
def send_alert(temp: float, humidity: float) -> None:
    """Send email alert when temperature is too high."""
    msg = MIMEText(f"ALERT!\nTemperature: {temp}°C\nHumidity: {humidity}%")
    msg["Subject"] = f"[HIGH TEMP] {temp}°C detected!"
    msg["From"]    = EMAIL_FROM
    msg["To"]      = EMAIL_TO
    with smtplib.SMTP_SSL("smtp.gmail.com", 465) as s:
        s.login(EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_PASS)
        s.sendmail(EMAIL_FROM, EMAIL_TO, msg.as_string())
    logging.info("Alert email sent!")
last_alert_time = 0   # prevent spam: only alert once every 30 minutes
while True:
    try:
        temp     = dht.temperature
        humidity = dht.humidity
        logging.info(f"Temp={temp}°C  Humidity={humidity}%")

# Check if alert needed and cooldown passed
        if temp > ALERT_TEMP and (time.time() - last_alert_time) > 1800:
            send_alert(temp, humidity)
            last_alert_time = time.time()
    except RuntimeError as e:
        # DHT sensors fail occasionally — just try again
        logging.warning(f"Sensor error (will retry): {e}")
    time.sleep(CHECK_INTERVAL)

import tflite_runtime.interpreter as tflite
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import time, argparse, logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
# ── Model Loading ──
def load_model(model_path: str) -> tflite.Interpreter:
    """Load TFLite model and allocate memory."""
    interp = tflite.Interpreter(model_path=model_path)
    interp.allocate_tensors()
    logging.info(f"Model loaded: {model_path}")
    return interp
def load_labels(labels_path: str) -> list[str]:
    """Load class label names."""
    with open(labels_path, "r") as f:
        return [line.strip() for line in f.readlines()]
# ── Image Preprocessing ──
def preprocess(image_path: str, size: int = 224) -> np.ndarray:
    """Resize and normalise image for MobileNet input."""
    img = Image.open(image_path).convert("RGB")
    img = img.resize((size, size))        # resize to 224x224
    arr = np.array(img, dtype=np.float32) # convert to numpy
    arr = arr / 255.0                     # normalise to [0, 1]
    arr = np.expand_dims(arr, axis=0)     # add batch dimension: (1, 224, 224, 3)
    return arr
# ── Inference ──
def classify(interp: tflite.Interpreter,
             image: np.ndarray,
             labels: list[str],
             top_k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Run inference and return top K predictions."""
    input_idx  = interp.get_input_details()[0]["index"]
    output_idx = interp.get_output_details()[0]["index"]
    interp.set_tensor(input_idx, image)
    t_start = time.perf_counter()
    interp.invoke()

latency_ms = (time.perf_counter() - t_start) * 1000
    scores = interp.get_tensor(output_idx)[0]  # shape: (1000,)
    top_indices = np.argsort(scores)[::-1][:top_k]
    results = [(labels[i], float(scores[i])) for i in top_indices]
    logging.info(f"Inference: {latency_ms:.1f}ms")
    return results
# ── Main ──
if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()

import paho.mqtt.client as mqtt
import anthropic, json, logging, os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from datetime import datetime
from collections import deque
load_dotenv()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(message)s")
# ── SETTINGS ──
NORMAL_TEMP_RANGE     = (15.0, 35.0)   # (min, max) degrees Celsius
NORMAL_HUMIDITY_RANGE = (30.0, 80.0)   # (min, max) percent
HISTORY_SIZE          = 10              # remember last 10 readings for context
# ── CLAUDE SETUP ──
claude = anthropic.Anthropic()
SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are an expert IoT system diagnostic engineer.
When given sensor readings, you:
1. Identify what is abnormal and why
2. List 2 possible physical causes (simple language)
3. Give 1 immediate action to take
4. Rate urgency: LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH / CRITICAL
Keep response under 5 sentences. Be direct.
"""
def ask_claude(current: dict, history: list) -> str:
    """Ask Claude to analyse an anomalous reading."""
    history_text = "\n".join([
        f"  {r['timestamp']}: {r['temperature']}°C, {r['humidity']}%"
        for r in list(history)[-5:]  # last 5 readings for context
    ])
    user_message = f"""
Current reading (ANOMALOUS):
  Temperature: {current['temperature']}°C (Normal: 15-35°C)
  Humidity: {current['humidity']}% (Normal: 30-80%)
  Time: {current['timestamp']}
Recent history (last 5 readings):
{history_text}

What is happening and what should I do?
    """
    response = claude.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=300,
        system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]
    )
    return response.content[0].text
# ── ANOMALY DETECTION ──
def is_anomaly(data: dict) -> bool:
    """Check if reading is outside normal range."""
    temp_lo, temp_hi = NORMAL_TEMP_RANGE
    hum_lo, hum_hi   = NORMAL_HUMIDITY_RANGE
    return (data["temperature"] < temp_lo or data["temperature"] > temp_hi or
            data["humidity"] < hum_lo or data["humidity"] > hum_hi)
# ── MQTT SETUP ──
history = deque(maxlen=HISTORY_SIZE)
def on_message(client, userdata, msg):
    data = json.loads(msg.payload.decode())
    history.append(data)
    if is_anomaly(data):
        logging.warning(f"ANOMALY DETECTED: {data}")
        print("\n" + "="*50)
        print("ANOMALY DETECTED!")
        print(f"Temperature: {data['temperature']}°C")
        print(f"Humidity:    {data['humidity']}%")
        print("\nAsking Claude AI for analysis...")
        analysis = ask_claude(data, history)
        print(f"\n  Claude Analysis:\n{analysis}")🤖
        print("="*50 + "\n")
    else:
        logging.info(f"Normal: {data['temperature']}°C, {data['humidity']}%")
client = mqtt.Client("ai_analyser")
client.on_message = on_message
client.connect("localhost", 1883)
client.subscribe("sensors/#", qos=1)

load_dotenv()
DB_PATH = "sensor_history.db"

@tool
def get_readings(sensor_type: str = "temperature", hours_ago: int = 1) -> str:
    """Get sensor readings from the last N hours. sensor_type: temperature or 
humidity."""
    since = datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(hours=hours_ago)
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn:
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT value, timestamp FROM readings
            WHERE sensor_type = ? AND timestamp > ?
            ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 50
        """, (sensor_type, since.isoformat())).fetchall()
    if not rows:
        return f"No {sensor_type} readings found in last {hours_ago} hour(s)"
    values = [r[0] for r in rows]
    return json.dumps({"count": len(rows), "min": min(values),
                      "max": max(values), "avg": round(sum(values)/len(values), 2),
                      "latest": values[0], "unit": "C" if sensor_type=="temperature" 
else "%"})
@tool

            SELECT COUNT(*) FROM readings
            WHERE sensor_type="temperature" AND value > ? AND timestamp > ?
        """, (threshold, since.isoformat())).fetchone()[0]

{days_ago} day(s)"
@tool
def get_current_reading() -> str:

SELECT sensor_type, value, timestamp FROM readings

import tflite_runtime.interpreter as tflite
import numpy as np
import adafruit_adxl34x, board, busio
import time, logging, paho.mqtt.client as mqtt, json
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
CLASSES = ["normal", "imbalance_fault", "bearing_fault"]
SAMPLE_RATE = 100  # readings per second
WINDOW_SIZE = 50   # use 50 readings per classification
# ── Sensor Setup ──
i2c   = busio.I2C(board.SCL, board.SDA)
adxl  = adafruit_adxl34x.ADXL345(i2c)
adxl.range = adafruit_adxl34x.Range.RANGE_2_G
# ── Model Setup ──
interp = tflite.Interpreter("vibration_model.tflite")
interp.allocate_tensors()
in_idx  = interp.get_input_details()[0]["index"]
out_idx = interp.get_output_details()[0]["index"]
# ── Feature Extraction ──
def extract_features(window: list) -> np.ndarray:
    """Convert raw XYZ readings to statistical features."""
    arr = np.array(window)         # shape: (50, 3)
    x, y, z = arr[:,0], arr[:,1], arr[:,2]
    magnitude = np.sqrt(x**2 + y**2 + z**2)
    features = [
        magnitude.mean(), magnitude.std(),
        magnitude.max(), magnitude.min(),
        np.percentile(magnitude, 25),
        np.percentile(magnitude, 75),
        np.sqrt(np.mean(magnitude**2)),  # RMS (root mean square)
        float(np.fft.fft(magnitude)[:3].real.mean()),  # dominant frequency
    ]
    return np.array([features], dtype=np.float32)  # shape: (1, 8)
# ── MQTT Setup ──
mq = mqtt.Client("predictor")
mq.connect("localhost", 1883)
mq.loop_start()
# ── Main Loop ──

window = []
while True:
    x, y, z = adxl.acceleration
    window.append((x, y, z))
    if len(window) >= WINDOW_SIZE:
        features = extract_features(window)
        interp.set_tensor(in_idx, features)
        interp.invoke()
        probs   = interp.get_tensor(out_idx)[0]
        pred_id = np.argmax(probs)
        pred    = CLASSES[pred_id]
        conf    = probs[pred_id]
        result = {"prediction": pred, "confidence": float(conf), "time": 
time.time()}
        logging.info(f"Prediction: {pred} ({conf*100:.1f}%)")
        mq.publish("predictions/vibration", json.dumps(result))
        if pred != "normal":
            logging.warning(f"FAULT DETECTED: {pred}!")
            mq.publish("alerts/vibration", json.dumps(result), qos=1)
        window = []  # reset window
    time.sleep(1/SAMPLE_RATE)

4.1 The Most Common Mistakes — Telugu/Hindi Speakers
Mistake 1: Missing Articles (a, an, the)
Telugu and Hindi do not have articles. So Telugu and Hindi speakers often drop them in English. This makes  
writing sound robotic and unprofessional.
  WRONG: ✗ I built sensor system for factory.
  RIGHT: ✓ I built a sensor system for a factory.
  WRONG: ✗ We need to restart server.
  RIGHT: ✓ We need to restart the server.
  WRONG: ✗ This is important concept in machine learning.
  RIGHT: ✓ This is an important concept in machine learning.
  RULE: 📐 Use "a" before consonant sounds (a sensor, a model, a database). Use "an" before vowel 
sounds (an algorithm, an IoT device, an API). Use "the" when you are talking about a specific thing both 
you and the reader know about.
Mistake 2: Wrong Verb Tense in Technical Writing
Technical documents (READMEs, reports) use PRESENT SIMPLE for things that are always true. Use PAST  
SIMPLE for what you did in a project. Use PRESENT PERFECT for recent achievements.

Chapter 6: How Neural Networks Actually Work
Most students think neural networks are mysterious black boxes. They are not. They are just mathematical  
functions with many parameters. Let us understand this properly.
6.1 What is a Neuron? (The Simplest Possible Explanation)
A biological neuron in your brain receives signals from other neurons, adds them up, and if the total is strong 
enough, it fires and sends a signal forward.
An artificial neuron works exactly the same way:
● It receives numbers (inputs)
● It multiplies each input by a weight (how important is this input?)
● It adds all the weighted inputs together
● If the total passes a threshold, it "fires" — outputs a non-zero number
  ANALOGY — Voting System: 🔄 Imagine a committee deciding whether to raise an alarm. Each 
committee member (neuron) has a vote weight — the expert gets 3 votes, the junior gets 1 vote. 
Everyone votes yes or no. If the total weighted votes exceed a threshold, the alarm fires. That is exactly 
how a neuron works.
# A single artificial neuron in Python (simplified)
def neuron(inputs: list, weights: list, bias: float) -> float:
    """
    inputs:  [temperature, humidity, vibration]  ← sensor readings
    weights: [0.8, 0.3, 0.9]  ← learned importance of each input
    bias:    -0.5  ← adjusts the threshold
    """
    # Step 1: Multiply each input by its weight and sum
    weighted_sum = sum(x * w for x, w in zip(inputs, weights)) + bias
    # Step 2: Apply activation function (ReLU: if negative, output 0)
    output = max(0, weighted_sum)
    return output

                weights=[0.8, 0.3, 0.9],
                bias=-0.5)
print(f"Neuron output: {result:.3f}")  # → 1.178 (fires!)
6.2 What is a Neural Network? (Neurons Working Together)
A neural network is just many neurons connected in layers. Each neuron in one layer connects to all neurons in 
the next layer.
  ANALOGY — Factory Assembly Line: 🔄 Layer 1 workers look at raw material (raw sensor data) and 
extract basic features. Layer 2 workers receive layer 1 outputs and detect patterns in those features. 
Layer 3 workers receive layer 2 outputs and make a final decision. This is a 3-layer neural network.
For your AIoT sensor classifier:
● Input layer: 8 features extracted from vibration window (mean, max, min, std, RMS, etc.)
● Hidden layer 1: 64 neurons detect basic patterns in the features
● Hidden layer 2: 32 neurons detect more complex combinations
● Output layer: 3 neurons — one per class (normal, imbalance, bearing_fault)
● The class with the highest output neuron value = the prediction
6.3 What is Training? (How Weights Are Learned)
When you first create a neural network, all weights are random — the network predicts nonsense. Training is 
the process of adjusting the weights until the network predicts correctly.
  ANALOGY — Tuning a Radio: 🔄 Imagine tuning an old radio to find a station. You turn the dial slightly, 
listen to see if it got better or worse, then turn it in the right direction. Training a neural network is the 
same: adjust weights, check if prediction got better or worse, adjust again. Do this millions of times.
The training process in 5 steps:
Step 1: Forward pass — Input goes through the network → produces a prediction
Step 2: Calculate loss — Compare prediction to correct answer → compute the error (loss)
Step 3: Backward pass (backpropagation) — Calculate how much each weight contributed to the error
Step 4: Update weights — Move each weight in the direction that reduces the error (gradient descent)
Step 5: Repeat — Do this for all training examples, many times (epochs)
  NOTE: 📌 You do not need to implement backpropagation yourself. PyTorch does it automatically with 
loss.backward(). This is the biggest magic of deep learning frameworks — autograd. Understand what it 
does, not how it works internally.

6.4 Why Does TFLite Exist? (The Edge AI Problem)
A trained PyTorch model is very large — ResNet50 is 98MB. Running it requires:
● 512MB+ RAM for model weights and activations
● A modern CPU or GPU
● Python + PyTorch installed (500MB+ of libraries)
A Raspberry Pi 4 has 4GB RAM, but other edge devices like ESP32 have only 512KB. Even Pi 4 would struggle  
with large models. TFLite solves this.
  ANALOGY — Packing a Suitcase: 🔄 Your full wardrobe (PyTorch model) is 20kg — too heavy for the 
flight. So you pack only essential clothes (TFLite conversion) and compress them tightly (quantisation). 
Same clothes, much lighter, fits in cabin bag.

6.5 INT8 Quantisation — Simple Explanation
Normal PyTorch uses 32-bit floating point numbers (FP32). Each weight is stored as a number like  
0.73842619... (32 bits = 4 bytes).
INT8 quantisation converts these to 8-bit integers: 0.73842619 → 59 (using a scale factor). 1 byte instead of 4 
bytes = 4x smaller.
  ANALOGY — Approximating a Price: 🔄 The exact price of a product is ₹847.73. For quick mental math 
you round it to ₹850. You lost a tiny bit of precision (₹2.27) but you gained massive speed in calculation. 
INT8 quantisation does the same to model weights.
# How to quantise your PyTorch model to INT8 TFLite

# First: you already have model.onnx from PyTorch export

# Then: convert ONNX → TF SavedModel → TFLite

# Enable quantisation

# Provide representative data so quantisation knows value ranges

    for i in range(100):
        # Yield batches of your actual sensor data
        yield [training_data[i:i+1].astype("float32")]
converter.representative_dataset = representative_dataset
converter.target_spec.supported_ops = [tf.lite.OpsSet.TFLITE_BUILTINS_INT8]
converter.inference_input_type  = tf.int8
converter.inference_output_type = tf.int8
# Convert and save
tflite_model = converter.convert()
with open("model_int8.tflite", "wb") as f:
    f.write(tflite_model)

7.3 I2C Protocol — How Multiple Sensors Share Two Wires
I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) is a protocol that allows many sensors to be connected to just TWO wires (SDA  
and SCL). Each sensor has a unique address (like a house number).
  ANALOGY — Shared Telephone Line: 🔄 I2C is like an old party telephone line where many houses share 
one line. When the Pi wants to talk to the temperature sensor, it first says the sensor's house number 
(address 0x77). Only that sensor responds. All others ignore the message.

# 50: -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 57 -- -- -- -- -- -- -- --
# 70: -- -- -- -- -- -- -- 77 
#
# 0x57 = ADXL345 vibration sensor
# 0x77 = BME280 temperature/pressure sensor
# Both on the SAME two wires (SDA=GPIO2, SCL=GPIO3)
7.4 Understanding UART — For GPS and GSM Modules
UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter) is the simplest serial protocol. Two wires: TX (transmit)  
and RX (receive). Used for GPS modules, GSM/4G modules, and debug consoles.
  NOTE: 📌 Important: Cross the wires. Your Pi TX connects to sensor RX. Your Pi RX connects to sensor 
TX. Think of it as two people talking — one's mouth (TX) connects to the other's ear (RX).

# /dev/ttyAMA0 is the hardware UART on Raspberry Pi
# Baud rate 9600 is standard for GPS modules
gps = serial.Serial("/dev/ttyAMA0", baudrate=9600, timeout=1)
while True:

            lon = float(parts[5]) / 100

9.1 The 4 Most Effective Study Techniques (Research-Backed)
Technique 1: Active Recall (Most Effective)
Instead of re-reading: close the book and try to recall what you just learned from memory.
  ANALOGY — Lifting Weights: 🔄 Reading is like watching someone else lift weights — you do not get 
stronger. Active recall is actually lifting the weights yourself — your brain struggles and gets stronger.

Technique 2: Spaced Repetition (Anki)
You forget things in a predictable curve (Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve). Spaced repetition shows you each card 
just before you would forget it — dramatically increasing retention with less time.
Without Anki With Anki (Spaced Repetition)

Re-study 2 days later — remember only 30% Anki shows cards you are forgetting — 85% retention

Technique 3: The Feynman Technique
Richard Feynman was a Nobel Prize winning physicist. His study method: if you cannot explain it simply, you do 
not understand it yet.
Step 1: Choose a concept — Example: INT8 quantisation
Step 2: Explain it simply — Write/speak as if explaining to a 12-year-old. Use analogies.
Step 3: Find the gaps — Where do you struggle to explain? Those are your weak spots.
Step 4: Go back and fill gaps — Re-study only the parts you could not explain.
Step 5: Simplify further — Remove jargon. If you need jargon to explain it, you do not understand it 
deeply enough.
Apply this for your Sunday AI sessions: after learning a new tool, spend 10 minutes explaining it to yourself (or 
record a short voice note) using zero technical jargon.
Technique 4: Interleaving
Instead of studying one subject for 3 hours, alternate between subjects every 45-60 minutes. Research shows 
interleaving improves long-term retention by 40% compared to blocked practice.
